clue.text: See 1 down
Are you texting in tweets, having got confused? It's hard to say

indicators.note: confused tells us the gathered letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: in text-message shorthand 'are you' is written as the letters R and U
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's text-speak tweets have become muddled and hard to read out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' scrambles RU (text-speak for 'are you') with IN, TWEETS and GOT; 'having' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tongue twister is a phrase deliberately difficult to pronounce, so it is literally hard to say.

clue.text: One unit's out of place? Yes and no

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are disarranged, so this signals an anagram

parts.note: read as 'unit is', giving the letters of UNITS

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a single unit is misplaced, and gets an equivocal answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' rearranges I and UNITS. The answer means 'in place', so the anagram that is out of place gives something in place: hence 'Yes and no'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means in its original position, so it is both out of place (as an anagram) and in place: an equivocal reply.

clue.text: Sort of policy that's beneath Nick Clegg?

explanation.surface: A political quip about the sort of policy below Nick Clegg's notice.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg led the Liberal Democrats, Britain's third-largest party after the Conservatives and Labour, so the party sits beneath its leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor insurance covering only damage to others is called this kind of cover; the Lib Dems were the UK's third force in politics.

clue.text: Shade round bottom of willow tree

indicators.note: round says the colour word encloses the other piece

parts.note: roan is a colour, a shade of reddish or greyish brown seen in horses

indicators.note: bottom of picks the last letter of the next word, as this is a down clue

explanation.surface: A colour is described as going round the base of a willow tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The rowan, or mountain ash, is a small tree with red berries.

clue.text: "Pontiac hit by 1 across", say

indicators.note: 1 across is a twister, and letters hit by a twister are tossed about into a new order

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline line about a Pontiac car struck by a tornado.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit by 1 across' (a twister) scrambles PONTIAC; the whole quoted phrase is itself an example of the answer, as under a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: Words printed beneath a news photograph, like this quoted line, form a title or explanatory caption.

clue.text: Annoyed about one social worker's role, say

indicators.note: about says the word for annoyed goes round the next piece

parts.note: annoyed means cross
one is the Roman numeral I
the ant is a social insect and a worker, read as 'social worker is'

explanation.surface: Someone is cross about one social worker's job description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'role, say' points to a word that sounds like role: the bread roll, of which this pastry is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: This French pastry is a kind of bread roll, and roll sounds the same as role.

clue.text: Kiss head off spot

indicators.note: head off removes the first letter of the word for spot

parts.note: a speck is a tiny spot

explanation.surface: An instruction to kiss away a spot on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A peck is a quick light kiss.

clue.text: As one child under 11 hugs sister

indicators.note: in a down clue, under means this piece comes after the rest
hugs says the two ones wrap round the word for sister

parts.note: the figures 1 and 1 are read as two Roman numerals I
a sister in religion is a nun
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A child under eleven gives a sister a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like the cross-reference to UNTIDINESS but is read as I I.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing things together, simultaneously, is acting as one, in harmony.

clue.text: Yankee editor briefly edited the Observer, unassisted

indicators.note: edited means rearranged, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
ED is the usual short form for editor

explanation.surface: An American editor briefly took charge of the Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper, which the surface uses; in the definition it is the eye that observes without lenses.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing something with no telescope or microscope is observing with the unaided eye.

clue.text: Groundhog Day in court, Charlie boy?

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them
Chuck is a familiar form of the boy's name Charles, or Charlie

explanation.surface: A film title, Groundhog Day, being discussed in court with a lad named Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groundhog Day' reads as the film, but Groundhog alone is the definition and Day gives D.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodchuck is another name for the North American groundhog, a burrowing marmot.

clue.text: Regularly not fit to eat soup for starters in American mess

indicators.note: in says the gathered pieces go inside the abbreviation for American
regularly takes every other letter of the words that follow

parts.note: to eat is to dine

indicators.note: for starters takes the first letter of the word soup

explanation.surface: Soup unfit to eat in an American mess hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' picks N, T, I from 'not fit'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is a state of disorder, the lack of tidiness.

clue.text: Time? It often flies

explanation.walkthrough: BIRD is British slang for a prison sentence, from rhyming slang 'birdlime' for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing bird is slang for serving a jail term; and a feathered creature usually flies.

clue.text: Fish eaten (except Wednesday) with a bit of 27 tripe

parts.note: cod is a fish

indicators.note: except says the abbreviation for Wednesday is taken away from the word for eaten

parts.note: swallowed means eaten

indicators.note: a bit of takes just the first letter of the answer to clue 27

explanation.surface: Fish eaten on every day but Wednesday, with a bit of pickle and tripe.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is slang for nonsense, as is this British word for rubbish talk.

clue.text: As a result of this, finds "Aha!" cry reverberating around Goole perhaps

definitions.text: As a result of this, finds "Aha!" cry reverberating around Goole perhaps

indicators.note: letters reverberating around are bounced about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; Goole is a town in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Someone digging near Goole cries 'Aha!' on making a find.
explanation.walkthrough: Goole is a town in East Yorkshire, England. The anagram of AHA, CRY and GOOLE gives the science whose finds prompt that cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Excavating ancient remains is the discipline that unearths finds and prompts cries of discovery.

clue.text: "Clotted cream's first to have gone off, Mr.Jones"

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word cream
gone off means turned bad, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Aled Jones is a Welsh singer, famous as a boy soprano

explanation.surface: Someone tells a Mr Jones that the clotted cream has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: Aled Jones is a Welsh singer and broadcaster known in Britain for 'Walking in the Air'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clotted means thickened into lumps, which is what congealed describes.

clue.text: Cat circumnavigating ocean capsizes as one gains momentum

indicators.note: in a down clue, capsizes turns the assembled letters upside down
circumnavigating means going round, so the cat word encloses the ocean word

parts.note: puss is a cat
the deep is the ocean

explanation.surface: A cat sailing round the world capsizes when its boat picks up speed.
explanation.walkthrough: PUS(DEEP)S read upward gives the answer; 'as one' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To go faster is to accelerate, which is gaining momentum.

clue.text: Chair and cot knocked over with feet being the long and the short of it

definitions.text: with feet being the long and the short of it

indicators.note: furniture knocked over lies in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chair and a cot are tipped over by someone's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: In poetry a trochee is a metrical foot of one long (stressed) syllable followed by one short.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse in feet of a long syllable then a short one is described with this metrical adjective.

clue.text: Complaint from fairy to fool involves Shakespeare's leading characters

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology
taken as written
nit is British slang for a fool

indicators.note: leading characters takes the first letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's leading characters, from fairy to fool, are bothered by an ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests A Midsummer Night's Dream's fairies and fools, but 'leading characters' gives the initials I and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflammation of the abdominal lining is a serious medical complaint.

clue.text: Use force to control opening offer in topless joint

indicators.note: in says the first letter of offer goes inside
topless removes the first letter, in this down clue the top

parts.note: a splice is a joint made by joining two ends

indicators.note: opening takes the first letter of offer

explanation.surface: An opening offer is made in a topless bar.
explanation.definitionFit: To police something is to keep it under control, enforcing order.

clue.text: Fever Pitch essentially has a variety of pushy characters

indicators.note: essentially takes the central letter of the word pitch
a variety of means the letters are arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Nick Hornby's football book Fever Pitch has many pushy characters in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fever Pitch' reads as the title of Nick Hornby's football memoir, but Fever is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Typhus is an infectious disease marked by high fever.

clue.text: Every single part of a river bar its source

indicators.note: bar its source means without its first letter

parts.note: a reach is a stretch of river

explanation.surface: Every part of a river, except where it rises, is described.
explanation.definitionFit: Each refers to every one individually, every single one.

clue.text: Slanderous article after female made out with politician

indicators.note: after places the article behind the rearranged letters
out means the letters are worked out into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a is the indefinite article
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A woman went out with a politician, and the article about it was libellous.
explanation.definitionFit: Slanderous speech damages a reputation, which is exactly what defamation is.

clue.text: Greek river with body of water rising

indicators.note: rising in a down clue reads the pieces upward

parts.note: the Po is a river in Italy
a sea is a body of water

explanation.surface: A Greek river swells as the water level rises.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek storyteller famous for his fables.

clue.text: Small bottle without a name

indicators.note: without says the letter named is taken out

parts.note: a phial is a small bottle

explanation.surface: A little bottle lacks a label.
explanation.definitionFit: Phil is a man's first name, short for Philip.

clue.text: Spooner's eponymous heroine retails these?

indicators.note: Spooner's tells us to swap the opening sounds of the two words

parts.note: She is the title heroine of H. Rider Haggard's novel She
retails means sells

explanation.surface: A title character who sells goods at retail.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue recalls the tongue twister 'She sells sea shells', tying back to 1 down/1 across.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the shells sold in the old tongue twister, the item she retails.

clue.text: Port for city of Newcastle? It hardly has what's needed

indicators.note: has what's needed says the words contain the answer

explanation.surface: Asking whether Newcastle has a port, and suggesting it barely has what it needs.
explanation.walkthrough: Leith is the port district of Edinburgh in Scotland; it runs through 'NewcastLE IT Hardly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Leith serves as the harbour for the Scottish capital, Edinburgh.

clue.text: Drunk that's chosen to be legless? On the contrary

indicators.note: on the contrary reverses the sense, so the leg is put in rather than removed

parts.note: picked means chosen
legless suggests removing a leg, abbreviated L as in cricket

explanation.surface: Is the drunk person chosen because they are legless?
explanation.walkthrough: Legless is British slang for very drunk; instead of losing L (leg) the chosen word gains one.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickled is slang for intoxicated, much like legless.

clue.text: Sprinkles Lord's pitch, preventing openers getting stuck in

indicators.note: getting stuck in says the opening letters are put inside the word for lords

parts.note: lords are peers; read as a plural, not the cricket ground

indicators.note: openers takes the first letters of pitch and preventing

explanation.surface: Rain sprinkles the Lord's cricket pitch, keeping the opening batsmen from getting started.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is London's famous cricket ground and openers are the first two batsmen; here Lord's means peers.
explanation.definitionFit: To pepper something is to sprinkle or scatter over it.
